title: In the same store at the same moment, your eggs might cost 23% more than the person next to you
dek: Algorithms have broken the old mechanism where comparison shopping kept prices in check: RealPage's software lets thousands of landlords coordinate rent increases without meeting, and Instacart quietly charges different prices for the same products based on customer identity.
why: A 25-minute interview packed with case studies: RealPage, Walmart patents, Delta Air Lines, Instacart experiments—each backed by specific numbers, no filler.
who: If you shop online and compare prices, are renting or negotiating rent, or care about antitrust and consumer protection.

points.h: Pricing has become a discipline of algorithmic engineering, not retail intuition
points.body: Lindsay Owens explains that pricing used to be simple: calculate cost, add profit, print a label, done. Now companies hire pricing consultants, physicists, and acquire AI firms outright—all to precisely engineer extraction from consumers' wallets. Her new book Gouged catalogs the old pricing tricks now amplified by technology.

points.h: Algorithms enable price coordination among competitors who never meet
points.body: Price-fixing used to require gathering rivals in a room, with constant risk of defection—affordable only in oligopolies with few players. But in rental housing, with thousands of landlords, RealPage's YieldStar software does the coordinating: landlords share unit type, amenities, pricing; the software suggests rent levels; many default to accepting them. The Department of Justice filed price-fixing charges in late 2024 after a federal raid on an Atlanta developer.

points.h: Seventy-five percent industry concentration provides fertile ground for pricing manipulation
points.body: Owens notes that 75% of US industries are more concentrated today than a generation ago. This consolidation creates conditions for hidden pricing: if consumers can easily cross the street for a cheaper alternative, companies can't easily exploit them. But as competition shrinks and comparison shopping becomes impossible—because prices vary by person—algorithmic pricing techniques flourish.

points.h: Retailers price-discriminate based on your car and shopping behavior
points.body: Owens catalogs data companies already collect or are trying to collect: Walmart filed a patent analyzing before-and-after vehicle suspension images to infer purchase weight; firms track children's ages to time product-recommendation ads; e-commerce sites use IP address to estimate regional household income; Expedia charged different prices for the same hotel room depending on location-inferred visitor income. Walmart's 2023 patent is explicit: when connected e-scan checkout detects tuna in a shopping cart, the mayonnaise price for that same cart rises.

points.h: Companies tell investors, patent offices, and consumers completely different stories
points.body: Owens' organization reviewed Delta Air Lines' investor earnings calls and found Delta discussing its arrangement with Israeli AI firm Fetcher to raise ticket prices. Delta initially gave Fetcher control over 1% of ticket pricing; seeing results, it scaled to 20% by year-end. Corporations maintain three separate narratives: one for shareholders, one for the patent office, one for the public.

points.h: One shopping cart, one store, one moment—but prices differ by 23%
points.body: Owens' organization and Consumer Reports recruited 400 volunteers to visit the same Instacart pickup location at the same time with 23 identical items in their carts and take screenshots. Nearly 75% of products showed different prices, with gaps reaching 23%—translating to roughly $1,200 per year in extra costs for an average household. After media coverage, Instacart's stock fell; the FTC and New York's attorney general both opened investigations; two weeks later, Instacart pledged same-time same-place same-price.

points.h: Calls to redistribute wealth through pricing don't describe what companies actually do
points.body: When companies defend personalized pricing by saying ‘we charge wealthy areas more and low-income areas less, for equity,’Owens calls this ‘corporate Robin Hoodism’and disputes it. The actual strategy is to extract the maximum from every person—low-income segments get squeezed less, not spared. Willingness to pay doesn't track income anyway: a parent rushing to a funeral or buying fever medicine for a sick child will exceed their income-suggested price ceiling; companies will eventually learn to capture these emotional moments.

points.h: AI shopping agents gaining wallet control raises unknown consumer risks
points.body: Owens reflects that the internet and e-commerce once promised transparency and buyer leverage, yet the reality exposed in this book is the opposite—technologies introduced opacity and manipulation, breaking earlier promises. Next comes agentic commerce and AI shopping assistants. Meta's Muse, for instance, claims to cancel unwanted subscriptions for users. But new risks follow: What data will these agents see? Once an AI agent can directly withdraw from your account, will the outcome be consumer-beneficial or not? No one yet knows.
